one_line: Locally installed, self-hosted camera + edge-vision systems for small NJ general and specialty contractors: PPE/fall-hazard alerts, timestamped progress and delivery logs, and after-hours intrusion alerts, priced as a fixed monthly service instead of per-camera enterprise contracts.

problem.summary: Small contractors carry two uninsured-in-practice risks on every active site: fall and struck-by exposure that federal OSHA fines and state workers' comp rates price directly, and theft/vandalism of tools, materials and equipment that is rarely recovered. Today both are handled by hand: a superintendent walking the site, a phone camera roll for progress photos, paper delivery tickets, and (if anything) a consumer camera pointed at the gate that nobody reviews until after a loss. The evidence that cameras change safety behaviour in construction specifically is thin and mostly vendor-reported; the evidence that falls dominate both fatalities and citation exposure is strong and government-published.

evidence.fact: 1,075 of 5,283 U.S. work fatalities in 2023 were in construction; falls, slips and trips accounted for 39.2% (421) of all construction fatalities.

Construction accounted for 47.8% of all fatal falls, slips and trips in the U.S. in 2023; within construction, roofing contractors accounted for 26.0% (110 deaths) and residential building construction 14.7% (62 deaths).

Note on the two BLS releases: the CFOI news release counts 421 construction deaths from falls, slips and trips (39.2% of the 1,075 construction deaths), while the TED chart counts 423 construction fatalities from falls, slips and trips and states that 38.5% of construction deaths were due to falls, slips and trips. So construction fall deaths should be quoted as roughly 421-423 and the share as 38.5%-39.2%, depending on which release is used.

Other construction sub-trades with fall fatalities in 2023: painting and wall covering 29, framing 27, electrical 27, plumbing/HVAC 24, commercial and institutional building 18, drywall and insulation 13, masonry 12.

29 CFR 1926.501 (fall protection, construction) was OSHA's most-cited standard in calendar 2024 with 8,797 citations and $53.8 million in current penalties, the most of any standard, per a third-party analysis of the DOL OSHA enforcement dataset (federal and state-plan programs combined). OSHA's own FY-based Top-10 page could not be read from this environment, and FY counts differ from calendar-year counts.
The maximum federal OSHA penalty for a serious violation rose to $16,550 per violation and for willful/repeated violations to $165,514, effective 15 January 2025 (from $16,131 and $161,323).

A conference paper presented at the Annual Associated Schools of Construction International Conference (April 2019) analysing more than 15,000 construction-site theft incidents in the FBI's NIBRS data found contractors lost an average of about $6,000 per incident, trucks averaged about $42,000 and were recovered 55% of the time, and recovery across all stolen targets was under 7%.
NICB and the National Equipment Register estimate theft of heavy construction equipment costs $300 million to $1 billion per year in the U.S., excluding tool theft and damage during the theft.
evidence.year: estimate cited in 2022 article (underlying NICB/NER data older)

evidence.fact: A vendor survey of 739 construction project managers, supervisors, tradesmen and site foremen found 78% said their organization had experienced jobsite theft, with tools the top target (86%). The host blog page carries no publication date; the 2020 attribution comes from the report artwork embedded on the page ("TrueLook Jobsite Security Report 2020"). Vendor-run survey; directionally useful only.
evidence.year: survey report dated 2020 per the report artwork; host blog page undated

evidence.fact: Employers that had 10 or fewer employees company-wide at all times during the last calendar year do not need to keep OSHA injury and illness records (OSHA 300/300A/301) unless notified in writing, but all covered employers must still report fatalities, in-patient hospitalisations, amputations and eye losses under 1904.39.
evidence.year: current regulation (29 CFR 1904.1), read in the Cornell LII mirror of the CFR

evidence.fact: Progress and delivery documentation is still largely manual photo capture: the low end of the market is phone-based photo apps priced per user (CompanyCam Core $79/month for 1-2 users, Crew $149/month for 3 users, Scale $299/month; extra users $34/month).

buyers.size_where_it_matters: 5-50 staff; matters from the first crew working at height on more than one site at a time
buyers.why: Largest single share of construction fall deaths in 2023 (110 deaths, 26.0% of the construction total), and the trade most exposed to 1926.501 fall-protection citations. Progress-photo logging is also a core need for insurance and warranty disputes.

buyers.business_type: Residential building construction / homebuilders and remodelers
buyers.why: 62 fall deaths in 2023 (14.7% of construction fall deaths). Multiple scattered sites is exactly where a superintendent cannot walk every site daily, which is where remote visual checks pay.
27 fall deaths in 2023; work is inherently at height and open-edge, and fall protection remains OSHA's most-cited standard.

buyers.size_where_it_matters: 20-200 staff with multiple crews and service vans
buyers.why: 27 and 24 fall deaths respectively in 2023; larger specialty firms also have equipment yards and van/tool inventory at theft risk and are more likely to have a safety director who owns a budget.

buyers.business_type: Commercial and institutional building contractors (small GCs/CMs)
buyers.why: A GC is the party that controls site access, so it is the natural camera buyer; also the party most exposed to multi-employer citation and to owner/insurer requirements for site documentation.

buyers.business_type: Site preparation, excavation and utility contractors
buyers.size_where_it_matters: 10-100 staff with a yard full of iron
buyers.why: Highest-value mobile equipment per employee; theft of machines and trailers is the loss this segment actually feels, and yard + gate cameras are the cheapest available mitigation.

buyers.business_type: Masonry, drywall, painting and wall covering
buyers.why: Smaller fall-death counts (12, 13, 29 in 2023) but very high head-count per site, so PPE compliance imaging covers many workers per camera; lowest ability to pay, so best served by the cheapest tier.

Appliance alternative: AI Box Mini A (3 cameras, Safety Guard) $5,020 one-time, or $2,260 hardware + $45/camera/month

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Real-time no-hard-hat alerts and event search on Silarius X or existing cameras; managed in the same app as live view and playback.
existing_solutions.pricing: $8.00/camera/month PPE add-on, on top of the Advanced AI Package ($16.00/camera/month) on the same camera and a Silarius Cloud plan from $6.99/camera/month - about $31/camera/month all-in as listed

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Rented or customer-owned Axis cameras with a hosted platform, time-lapse, live view; cellular/satellite connectivity add-on per site.
existing_solutions.pricing: Platform from $79/camera/month; camera rental $39/month fixed, $89 PTZ, $139 panoramic; cellular from $60/month per site; installation quoted

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Waist-worn clip that detects worker falls and lets workers raise alarms over an on-site mesh network; zone-level worker location, mustering, plus EquipTag equipment tracking. Not a camera product; the main substitute for fall-event detection where cameras cannot see the worker.

gap_for_local_installer: The market is split between enterprise managed services that publish prices a small contractor cannot absorb (Evercam lists $500/month for its software service package, plus $500/month for each additional fixed-position camera and $3,700/month for a 4K kit; EarthCam and Samsara are quote-only) and cheap self-serve detectors that assume the customer has cameras, networking, someone to tune thresholds, and someone to read alerts. Those self-serve options are cheaper than enterprise but not trivial once fully costed: Silarius PPE is about $31/camera/month all-in on its listed stack, and ARSA's $48/camera/month Safety Guard module needs a four-camera minimum and a customer-supplied GPU server (or a $5,020 three-camera AI Box). Nobody local does the middle: site survey, camera placement for the actual fall/PPE geometry, calibration on that customer's footage for a week, a human-reviewed weekly report, and a truck that shows up when a camera dies. A Milltown-based installer can also bundle the things a cloud vendor will not: yard and gate cameras at the shop, delivery-ticket photo capture tied to the ticket, and integration with whatever phone-photo habit the crew already has (CompanyCam-class tools), at a flat $300-$900/site/month instead of $2,000+. Second-order gap: general contractors who must document safety for owners and insurers but have no in-house safety staff.

technical_approach.established_pattern: ONVIF/RTSP cameras -> PoE switch -> edge box on site running an object detector per frame (YOLO-family person/PPE classes) -> multi-object tracker to keep identities across frames -> zone and association rules (e.g. person with no hard-hat class overlapping them inside a defined work zone for more than N seconds) -> event clip + snapshot -> alert to supervisor phone/email -> nightly or on-demand review of low-confidence events by a small vision-language model, which writes a plain-language description for the log -> local recording with 14-30 day retention and a weekly PDF report. Recording and detection stay on site (no per-camera cloud bill); only alert clips and report images leave the network. This mirrors what Samsara, ARSA and Evercam do architecturally, minus the cloud per-camera pricing.

models_and_tools.name: Frigate (open source NVR)
models_and_tools.role: Camera ingest, motion gating, object detection, zones, event recording and MQTT alerts; supports ONNX/YOLO exports and OpenVINO/Hailo/NVIDIA accelerators. Note: it detects objects, it does not decide PPE compliance - the person-to-PPE association logic has to be written on top.

models_and_tools.name: Frigate hardware planning guidance
models_and_tools.role: Sizing rules for an on-site box: Intel CPU with AVX2, 4 GB RAM minimum with a dedicated detector, 8 GB practical, 16 GB for larger systems; hardware video decode matters as much as detection.

models_and_tools.name: YOLO-family detectors (Ultralytics YOLOv8/YOLO11 and derivatives)
models_and_tools.role: The workhorse for person, hard-hat, hi-vis vest, harness and lanyard classes; published PPE studies use YOLO variants, YOLACT and Efficient-YOLOv5 backbones.

models_and_tools.name: Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct
models_and_tools.role: Small vision-language model for exception review: describe an alert clip in words (for example two workers on the second-floor edge with no visible lanyard) so a non-technical superintendent can triage on a phone; the 2B dense variant is the edge-friendly size.

models_and_tools.name: LFM2.5-VL-3B (Liquid AI)
models_and_tools.role: Alternative edge VLM for the same exception-review role, with 1.6B and 450M variants for tighter devices; Liquid AI documents local deployment via llama.cpp, MLX and vLLM.

models_and_tools.name: llama.cpp
models_and_tools.role: Runtime to serve the quantised VLM on the on-site box or a small office GPU, keeping exception descriptions local.

models_and_tools.name: Home Assistant
models_and_tools.role: Optional glue for small contractors who want alerts, dashboards and automations (SMS, siren, gate relay) without a custom app; Frigate integrates via MQTT.

technical_approach.fine_tuning_needed: Partly. Generic person detection works out of the box. Everything that makes money - hard-hat vs. no hard-hat, hi-vis colour, harness worn vs. lanyard clipped to an anchor, person inside an excavation exclusion zone - needs either a fine-tuned detector or per-site rule calibration. Public PPE datasets (e.g. SHWD, the dataset behind ARSA's 98.2% vendor claim) get you most of the way; the rest comes from 1-2 weeks of footage from the customer's own cameras, angles and lighting. A small VLM can cover exceptions without fine-tuning but is too slow/expensive per frame on a Jetson-class box to replace the detector.
technical_approach.data_needed: 500-2,000 labelled frames per site from the actual camera positions, stratified across morning/afternoon/night, sun glare, rain, and winter low sun; hard negatives (workers carrying hard hats, hoods, bicycle helmets, hi-vis on a truck seat) to cut false positives; 2-4 weeks of unlabelled footage for threshold tuning and zone masks; ground-truth spot audits by the superintendent to measure precision/recall against reality rather than a benchmark. Labelling effort is the main variable cost.

measured_outcomes.finding: Computer-vision harness detection reached 80% precision and 98% recall for identifying workers not wearing a harness, with worker detection at 99% precision / 95% recall.
measured_outcomes.sample: Construction-site image dataset; abstract does not state dataset size

measured_outcomes.finding: An Efficient-YOLOv5 harness-use detector reported 97.7% precision, 89.3% recall and 94% mAP.

PPE detection on surveillance-camera footage scored 92.36% mAP on one test set but only 66.70% on a second - a concrete demonstration that accuracy collapses when the site, camera or lighting changes.
measured_outcomes.sample: Two test sets of surveillance-camera footage (sizes per paper)

measured_outcomes.finding: A YOLACT + DeepSORT PPE-monitoring framework reached 91.3% accuracy for PPE-wearing status and 66.4 mAP@50 for detection.

A drone-plus-deep-learning work-at-height system reported 90% overall accuracy (97.2% precision, 90.2% recall) for harness, lifeline and helmet checks, with roughly 12 seconds average violation-detection time.
measured_outcomes.sample: Field trials on real construction sites plus a controlled lab environment, as described in the paper

measured_outcomes.finding: CCTV does reduce crime in some settings but not as a stand-alone measure. Welsh & Farrington's earlier review (44 evaluations) found a 16% overall reduction driven by a 51% reduction in car-park schemes; the 2019 update by Piza, Welsh, Farrington and Thomas (80 evaluations, 76 meta-analysed) found about a 13% overall reduction and about a 37% reduction across 8 car-park evaluations, and reports that schemes deploying multiple interventions alongside CCTV generated larger effect sizes than single-intervention schemes. The effect is therefore not attributable to cameras alone, and the evidence comes from car parks and public space, not construction sites.
measured_outcomes.sample: 80 CCTV evaluations reviewed, 76 in the meta-analysis; 8 car-park evaluations in the 2019 update

measured_outcomes.finding: Construction theft recovery across all stolen targets was under 7% of incidents (trucks the outlier at 55%), which is the baseline cameras would have to beat for theft to be a paying use case.
measured_outcomes.study_type: conference proceedings (Annual Associated Schools of Construction International Conference, April 2019)

measured_outcomes.finding: Smartvid.io reported that its model predicted 20% of incidents at about 80% accuracy on three years of unseen data, and the customer (Suffolk) estimated $1.4M-$3.6M in annual avoided incident costs across a 50-project portfolio. This is a projected saving, not an observed incident reduction.
measured_outcomes.sample: One contractor, 50-project portfolio, 3 years of historical data

measured_outcomes.finding: ARSA reports 98.2% of hard-hat decisions correct and 0.5% of helmet wearers wrongly flagged on the SHWD set, with the system declining to decide on 32% of heads (reported as unknown, never as a violation), and 94.1% of hard-hat decisions correct on SH17. Vendor-run benchmark on public datasets, out of the box - not a site deployment.
measured_outcomes.sample: SHWD test set 667 images / 2,221 heads; SH17 test set 1,620 images / 2,457 heads

measured_outcomes.finding: No study found that isolates a construction-site camera installation and reports a measured reduction in injuries or OSHA recordables. The nearest vendor assertion is Smartvid.io's December 2020 funding release, which states its platform 'cut incident rates by as much as 50 percent' over the prior 12 months for three named large contractors; the release gives no incident counts, no control group and no site-level detail, so it is an unverifiable vendor claim, not a measured outcome.
measured_outcomes.sample: n/a - no sample, counts or control group disclosed

legal_privacy.issue: Audio recording of workers on site
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: N.J.S.A. 2A:156A-4(d) makes interception lawful only where the person is a party to the communication or one party has given prior consent. A fixed camera with a live microphone recording conversations among workers, with no party consent, is the risky configuration. Default recommendation: disable audio entirely.

legal_privacy.issue: Cameras covering areas where people undress or expect privacy (site trailers, porta-john approaches, changing areas)
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: N.J.S.A. 2C:14-9 makes it a crime of the third or fourth degree to observe, film or record a person without consent where a reasonable person would not expect to be observed and intimate parts may be exposed; prior notice plus a lawful purpose is an affirmative defense. Cameras must be aimed away from these areas.

legal_privacy.issue: Whether New Jersey requires employers to give notice before ordinary video-only workplace cameras
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: No New Jersey statute or regulation requiring general employer notice for ordinary fixed video cameras was located. Notice is still recommended as the practical defense under 2C:14-9(d) and as the cheapest way to avoid a monitoring grievance. Treat as unconfirmed rather than settled.

legal_privacy.issue: Face recognition / biometric identification of workers
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: No enacted New Jersey biometric-privacy statute specific to employers was found as of November 2026. A4981/S4075 (workplace electronic monitoring including biometric tools) is pending, and A3929 (biometric surveillance at business premises, consumer-facing) passed the Assembly in March 2026 and was referred to a Senate committee. ARSA's product design (video stays local, face recognition optional and licensed separately) is a reasonable template. Recommendation: do not sell face recognition in this pilot.

legal_privacy.issue: Tracking devices on employee-used vehicles (relevant if cameras are mounted on trucks or equipment)
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: New Jersey P.L. 2021, c.449 requires written notice for use of a tracking device on a vehicle; a fixed jobsite camera is outside that rule, a camera/telematics unit on a company truck an employee takes home is not.

legal_privacy.issue: Using cameras in a way that chills organizing or complaints about working conditions
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: Section 7 of the NLRA protects concerted activity; surveillance or the impression of surveillance of union or protected activity is an unfair labor practice. Cameras aimed at the gate or laydown yard are fine; cameras used to identify who talks to whom are not.

legal_privacy.issue: Which OSHA rules apply in New Jersey
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: New Jersey's OSHA-approved State Plan (PEOSH) covers state and local government employees only; private-sector contractors in Middlesex County are under federal OSHA jurisdiction, so 29 CFR 1926 and 1904 apply directly. The 2025 penalty rule also lists New Jersey among the state plans covering only state and local government employees.

legal_privacy.issue: Reporting obligations that a camera system could help or hurt
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: 29 CFR 1904.39 requires reporting work-related fatalities to OSHA within 8 hours and in-patient hospitalisations, amputations or losses of an eye within 24 hours (the in-patient case only counts where it involves care or treatment, not observation or diagnostic testing). Footage that shows the delay between an incident and the report becomes relevant evidence.

legal_privacy.issue: Drone-based progress capture over a site
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: Commercial drone flights fall under FAA Part 107 (remote pilot certificate, aircraft registration, visual line of sight, generally at or below 400 ft AGL, no flight over people outside an allowed category). This matches the well-known rule set but neither the FAA page nor eCFR could be read (403 / bot block), so it is listed as unconfirmed at source; airspace authorization may additionally be needed near Middlesex County airports/heliports.

legal_privacy.issue: Whether an NJ municipality or insurer can require site cameras
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: No statewide New Jersey camera mandate was found; the Uniform Construction Code (N.J.A.C. 5:23) does not impose a general camera requirement. A municipal ordinance, permit condition, fire official, owner or insurer can still require one, and NJ DCA fire-watch requirements for certain large new construction can be combined with site-security duties. Unconfirmed at the Milltown level.

legal_privacy.issue: Discoverability of footage in injury litigation and workers' comp claims
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: Footage becomes a record the contractor must keep and may have to produce; a system that records selectively, overwrites quickly and logs who accessed clips is safer than unlimited retention. (inference - no specific NJ rule verified on retention periods; no statutory retention period for private workplace video was located)

legal_privacy.issue: False accusation risk from automated PPE alerts
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: An alert that names a worker as non-compliant when the detector is wrong is a discipline and defamation exposure. Published cross-site accuracy drops (92.36% to 66.70% mAP) and a vendor benchmark that declines to decide on about a third of heads make this a live risk; mitigation is human review before any disciplinary use and never using the system as the sole basis for discipline. (inference from measured accuracy figures)

public: Trade mix: roofing (NAICS 238160) and residential builders (236115/236118) are the highest fall-death categories in BLS data - prioritize them.
Multiple active project addresses on the company website (a scattered-site contractor cannot walk every site daily).
Job postings for a safety director, site safety coordinator or CHSO - a company already spending on safety has a budget line to redirect.
OSHA inspection or citation history for the establishment (public enforcement data) - cited contractors are motivated buyers right after a citation.
Any public severe-injury report or news item about a fall or struck-by at one of their sites.
Google/Yelp reviews that mention jobsite mess, unsafe crews, no-shows, or damaged property - a proxy for supervision gaps (inference).
Equipment listings or fleet pages showing owned iron (excavators, skid steers, trailers) - yard value at risk from theft.
Insurance or owner requirements published in bid documents (some public bids require site documentation or monitoring).
Company size 15-200 employees: big enough to have multiple crews and a real workers' comp premium, small enough to have no in-house IT.
walk_in: Are the cameras on the fence/trailer real and recording, or dummy housings? Ask who reviewed the last incident.
Is there a written log of what happened after the last near-miss, or just a phone camera roll?
Who signs delivery tickets, and is there a photo of the load attached to the ticket?
Are hard hats and hi-vis actually worn at the gate at 7am, or only when the owner visits?
Is anyone working at height without a visible tie-off point, ladder extension or guardrail?
Is equipment left overnight at the site or hauled to a yard, and is the yard lit and covered?
Does the site trailer have power and internet, or would the system need LTE and solar?
How many active sites does the superintendent cover in a week, and how many hours are spent driving between them?

pilot.scope: One active site selected with the customer, 4-6 weeks. Install 3-4 PoE cameras: one at the gate/entrance, one covering the primary work-at-height face, one covering the material laydown/delivery area, one covering the equipment parking area. Deliver four functions: (1) hard-hat/hi-vis zone alerts to the superintendent's phone with a 60-second review clip; (2) a timestamped daily progress photo set at fixed camera positions plus a weekly time-lapse; (3) delivery verification - a timestamped gate photo of every truck and load, attached to the delivery ticket number; (4) after-hours person/vehicle alerts in the equipment zone. Audio disabled, face recognition off, signage posted, 30-day retention, weekly 1-page report with alert counts and reviewed outcomes.
pilot.hardware: 4 outdoor PoE IP cameras (commodity units, roughly $60-$250 each per a third-party cost guide) on a small PoE switch; on-site edge box (Jetson Orin Nano Super class at $249, or a mini-PC with Intel iGPU/OpenVINO) running Frigate with a fine-tuned YOLO PPE model plus a small VLM (Qwen3-VL-2B or LFM2.5-VL-3B quantised under llama.cpp) for exception descriptions; 2 TB SSD for 30-day retention; LTE router or customer Wi-Fi if the site has no service; small UPS; a mount/mast solution that does not require penetration where the site forbids it. Materials roughly $1,200-$2,500 at current component prices - inference from listed component prices, not a quote.
pilot.success_metric: Measured against a 1-week manual baseline on the same site: (a) alert precision of at least 80% on human-reviewed alerts (i.e. no more than 1 in 5 alerts judged wrong), (b) at least 90% of gate entries during work hours captured with a usable photo, (c) 100% of deliveries logged with a timestamped gate photo and ticket number, (d) median alert-to-phone latency under 60 seconds, (e) at least 3 supervisor interventions traceable to an alert in 4 weeks, (f) superintendent reports the weekly report saves at least 1 hour of walking/documenting per week. These are pilot design targets, not benchmarks from a published study.
pilot.cost_range: Roughly $6,000-$12,000 for a 4-6 week single-site pilot including hardware, install, labelling/calibration and weekly reporting (assumes 60-100 hours of setup and tuning at $75-$125/hour, 4 cameras, one site within 20 miles of Milltown). If the customer owns the cameras and network, $2,500-$5,000. Ongoing run rate after pilot: $400-$900 per site per month for hosting-free local operation plus monthly review and one truck roll, compared with Evercam's published $500/month software service package plus $500/month per additional fixed camera and $3,700/month for a 4K kit. Assumptions: no union site-access complications, site has power, customer provides a superintendent for 2 hours per week of ground truth.
pilot.assumptions: One site; 4 cameras; daylight and dusk operation only (no night PTZ work in pilot); site has 120V power at the trailer; cellular data plan available if no internet; customer can name one accountable reviewer; footage stays local; no audio; no face recognition; no drone flights.

fit_score.rationale: Sub-scores (demand 15/20, local buyers 12/15, ability to pay 10/15, technical feasibility 14/20, legal risk 7/15, defensibility 8/15) sum to 66/100. Demand is real and government-documented - falls, slips and trips were 39.2% of construction deaths in 2023 in the CFOI release (38.5% in the BLS TED piece; the two releases also differ by two deaths, 421 vs 423), 1926.501 is OSHA's most-cited standard at 8,797 calendar-2024 citations, and the serious-violation maximum is $16,550 since January 2025 - but it is demand for compliance, not for cameras; small contractors buy guardrails and training before they buy vision. Local buyers are plentiful in a county of Middlesex's size, but the addressable slice is firms with roughly 15-200 staff and multiple concurrent sites; at 10 or fewer employees the 29 CFR 1904.1 recordkeeping exemption removes the paperwork motive and budgets are thin (no verified county-level establishment count - see data_gaps - so this sub-score is held at 12 of 15 rather than 15). Ability to pay is the weak link: construction margins are thin, published enterprise pricing (Evercam $500/month software service package plus $500/month per additional fixed camera, $3,700/month 4K kit) is far above what a 25-person roofer will approve, which is exactly why a $400-$900/site/month local service can win - but the sale is long and evidence-based, and theft ROI depends on beating a 7% recovery baseline that cameras alone have not been shown to move. Technical feasibility is good with open tools (Frigate, YOLO PPE models, small VLMs) but published cross-site accuracy drops (92.36% to 66.70% mAP) mean calibration labour is unavoidable, and site power/network/weather are recurring service costs. Legal risk is moderate, not low: video-only with signage is comparatively safe in NJ, the 1904.1/1904.39 duties are clear, but audio recording (statutory civil liability under 2A:156A-4), face recognition (pending A4981/S4075, A3929), NLRA surveillance exposure, discoverability of footage and defamation/discipline risk from false positives all require contract-level discipline - hence 7 of 15 rather than 10. Defensibility is low-to-moderate: hardware and models are commodity and self-serve software sells for roughly $31/camera/month all-in (Silarius) to $48/camera/month plus a customer-supplied GPU server (ARSA); the moat is local installation, calibration on the customer's own footage, human-reviewed reporting and truck-roll reliability.

risks: Alert fatigue and false positives: published PPE accuracy falls sharply across sites (92.36% to 66.70% mAP), so an untuned deployment will annoy the superintendent within a week and get unplugged.
False accusation exposure: an automated no-hard-hat flag on the wrong worker creates discipline and defamation risk; human review must gate any disciplinary use.
Footage is discoverable evidence: a camera that captures a fall it did not prevent, or shows a supervisor ignoring a violation, can hurt the contractor in litigation and in the workers' comp claim.
Audio: any always-on microphone recording worker conversations is likely unlawful in NJ without consent (2A:156A-4) - a single mis-specified camera can create statutory civil liability.
Face recognition: no NJ employer biometric statute today, but pending bills (A4981/S4075, A3929) could retrofit obligations onto an installed base.
Camera hardware on an active site gets hit, stolen, unplugged or painted; uptime is a service cost, not a one-time install.
Power and connectivity: many small sites have no live service drop, so LTE data plans and solar/battery add recurring cost and failure modes.
Buyer ambiguity: on a GC-controlled site the specialty subcontractor cannot mount cameras, so the buyer is often the GC - a different (and slower) sales motion than the trade contractor.
Union sites: camera placement and any use that looks like productivity surveillance can trigger grievances even where safety is the stated purpose.
Seasonality and project churn: cameras must move every few months, which is labour-heavy and hard to price as a subscription.

Competition is cheap and getting cheaper: Silarius lists PPE at about $31/camera/month all-in and ARSA sells a 3-camera Safety Guard appliance outright for $5,020, while camera-agnostic platforms (Samsara SG1-G) make existing cameras smart. On a four-camera site the listed self-serve software costs about $124-$192/month, so a $400-$900/site/month service has to justify roughly 2-7x that price in labour and local accountability (inference from the listed prices).

Value proof is thin: no study isolates a construction camera deployment and shows measured injury reduction, so the sales case leans on citations, insurance and documentation rather than safety outcomes.
caveats: The strongest numbers here are about the size and cost of the problem (BLS fatalities, OSHA citations and penalties, NIBRS theft losses), not about cameras fixing it. Every construction-specific PPE accuracy figure comes from curated research datasets, and the one paper that tested on two surveillance sets showed a 25-point mAP drop between them - so a vendor benchmark (including ARSA's 98.2%, which is vendor-run and declines to decide on about a third of heads) should never be repeated as an expectation on a real site. The theft study is a conference paper, not a peer-reviewed journal article, though its NIBRS sample (15,000+ incidents) is the largest found. The theft ROI case is weak on current evidence: recovery is under 7% overall, and the systematic-review CCTV evidence is from car parks and public space, with larger effects where cameras were combined with other measures - not from construction sites. Several key vendor prices (EarthCam, Samsara, OpenSpace, Triax) are quote-only and could not be confirmed; the $130-$600+/camera/month band for proprietary camera services comes from a third-party guide published by a competing BYO-camera platform, not from the vendors themselves. Vendor outcome claims are rated Low throughout; the only quantified reduction figure offered by a vendor is Smartvid.io's 2020 statement of 'as much as 50 percent', which discloses no counts or control group and is reported here as unverified rather than as a range. osha.gov, faa.gov and ecfr.gov all returned HTTP 403 or bot blocks from this environment, so: OSHA's FY-based Top-10 counts are replaced here with a third-party analysis of the calendar-2024 DOL enforcement dataset (8,797 citations, $53.8M) because the FY figures could not be read; the FAA Part 107 rule set is marked unconfirmed for the same reason. The 29 CFR 1904.1 small-employer exemption and the 1904.39 reporting deadlines were read in full in the Cornell LII mirror of the CFR and are stated as read there. The OSHA penalty amounts ($16,550 serious, $165,514 willful/repeated) were read directly in the Federal Register inflation-adjustment rule. The two BLS releases differ slightly on construction fall deaths (421 and 39.2% in CFOI; 423 and 38.5% in TED), so both figures are reported rather than reconciled. The CCTV figures are read from a publicly hosted copy of the Piza et al. 2019 review (Criminology & Public Policy 18:135-159); the publisher's own pages returned 403. The TrueLook survey figures come from a vendor blog page with no publication date - the 2020 vintage is inferred from the embedded report artwork. Legal points are research findings, not legal advice, and the NJ legislative picture (biometric bills) is moving.
